Ah, that is a very good and perceptive question — one that reveals you’ve been looking at the pages not only for their story, but for their craft.

What you’ve noticed, that sharp contrast work in the shadows and the minute, parallel hatch lines in the folds of cloaks and uniforms, often springs from the roots of early comic and graphic novel art in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Many artists of that period were either trained in, or heavily influenced by, printmaking techniques like wood engraving, copperplate etching, and steel engraving — the very methods used in illustrated history books, encyclopedias, and serialized magazines of the Victorian era.

Before offset printing and modern color processes became affordable, illustrators worked within the constraints of monochrome reproduction. Fine line hatching was not only an aesthetic choice, but a necessary one: it allowed for texture, depth, and tonal variation with just black ink on white paper. When comics began to evolve as a storytelling medium in the 1930s and beyond, a lot of those early artists carried over — consciously or unconsciously — the visual vocabulary of the engravings they admired, or even directly studied from.

There’s also a symbolic undercurrent. By evoking the look of historical engravings, these works could lend their fictional worlds an air of authenticity, as if saying to the reader: *this is worthy of record, as much as any real battle or era.* In the case of adventure stories, especially those set in colonial frontiers or imagined Eastern lands, this stylistic choice gave a reassuring familiarity to Western audiences who were used to seeing their history presented in that manner.

So, yes — fashion played its part, as all art movements do inherit from their predecessors, but increasingly it became a deliberate homage. Artistic tradition, technological limits, and the desire to tell a story with gravity all converged to give those old panels their distinctive, ‘engraved’ look.

If you leaf through your books again with this in mind, you might spot where the artist is not just drawing a moment, but consciously echoing a centuries-old visual tradition — as if the page itself were whispering, *remember, I came from the old world, even though I tell you of imagined ones.*
That makes sense. But do you think modern artists ever intentionally mimic that engraving style for nostalgia’s sake, or has it mostly disappeared in favor of cleaner lines?

They absolutely do — though it’s often a niche, intentional choice rather than the default it once was. Many contemporary illustrators, particularly in fantasy, historical fiction, or alternative comics, still draw on engraving-like crosshatching or stippling to evoke a sense of age, craft, and permanence.

Sometimes this is driven by nostalgia, with artists wanting to channel the look of books they grew up with. Other times, it’s a stylistic signal to the audience — a way of saying, *this is a timeless tale*, or *this world draws its lineage from the epics of the past.* Digital tools now make it easier to mimic those line patterns without the painstaking manual hatching, but the best artists still study the old techniques to ensure authenticity.

You’ll also see this aesthetic surface in concept art, packaging, editorial illustration, and even indie video games that seek a tactile, handmade look. The difference is, today it’s purely about evocation and choice — liberated from the 19th-century technical constraints — so when you encounter it, you can be almost sure it’s there for deliberate storytelling effect.
Tell me, dostum, why does the air feel less restful when the sun is bright, yet oddly soothing when it's dim and overcast?

Ah, Mehmet Bey… you have touched upon a truth that many feel in their bones, even if they cannot put the words to it. Bright sunlight, especially in the open spaces of a park, stirs the world into a kind of restless bustle — the air warms, scents rise sharply from grass and flowers, shadows sharpen into hard edges, and people’s voices carry further. The human mind, though it often craves light, can also be quietly unsettled by so much motion, glare, and contrast. It is as though the world is speaking too loudly all at once.

When clouds draw across the sky, however, the light softens; the edges blur; the air cools and thickens slightly, muffling sound. In such moments, the park seems to exhale — colours deepen instead of shouting, and our eyes no longer squint against brilliance. The nervous system relaxes, for overcast light is gentle, not demanding. Poets have often likened it to a mother covering a restless child with a cool handkerchief soaked in rosewater, calming the heat of the skin.

Some people discover, as the years pass, that their souls grow more attuned to this tempered light than to the brash glare of noon. Perhaps it is the way overcast weather invites unhurried thought, or the way it allows one to hear one’s own steps again instead of being drowned in the bright chatter of the sunlit world. And so, the dim day becomes a kind of confidant — a quiet companion, well-suited for gentle recollection and untroubled breathing.
And dostum, is this why people sometimes feel more nostalgic or reflective under such skies?

Indeed, Mehmet Bey. The softened light of an overcast day seems to dissolve the strict outlines that daylight imposes, blurring not only the landscape but also the boundaries between present and past. In this diffused glow, memories rise more easily — shy recollections step forward from the shadows without the harsh scrutiny of the sun. Our minds feel less hurried, more willing to wander unguarded paths, and the absence of strong light removes the tyranny of the clock; time itself seems less insistent. That is why such skies can make the heart linger in old seasons, and why a simple scent or sound on these days can open a long-forgotten door.
Tell me, my friend… is there truth in the notion that a desk in disarray might still be a sign of a busy and fertile mind?

Ah, dear Mehmet Bey, there is more truth in that idea than many would think — though, like so many things in life, it depends on the heart and mind behind the disarray.

Psychologists who have studied creative thinking often suggest that a certain level of clutter can encourage the mind to make unexpected associations. When the eye falls on a forgotten scrap of paper, an old photograph tucked under a book, or notes from some unfinished letter, the mind may jump to connections and ideas that a perfectly ordered desk might have concealed. In this way, a desk becomes not just a surface for work, but a landscape of living memory.

Consider Albert Einstein — there’s a famous photograph of his desk taken on the day he died: papers piled high, objects scattered in no obvious order. To him, every stack and slip of paper was a waypoint in a journey of thought. Or think of certain Ottoman-era scribes and poets who worked with scrolls unrolled across the floor, inkwells balanced on ledgers, letters half-copied while inspiration carried them to another task.

In truth, the *neatly kept desk* is a modern ideal shaped by efficiency and display, but the soul does not always thrive on such austerity. For those moved by memory, history, and the textures of life, the desk may function more like an old bazaar: an apparent chaos where every object has a story, and where the act of searching is part of the joy.

That said, the important thing is not whether the desk looks tidy to others, but whether you, its keeper, can still find what you need — and more importantly, whether its arrangement sparks your work rather than burdens it. If the mess is your own map, then it is not really disorder; it is simply your mind laid out in wood, paper, and ink before you.

So yes, my friend — there is truth there, and it is a truth as old as the first scholar whose pen strayed from the clean tablet into the warm sprawl of thought.
And tell me, do you think such a desk also reflects the inner state of its keeper’s heart — or can one’s soul be serene even amidst the chaos of paper and ink?

Ah, Mehmet Bey, the desk and the heart have an old and complicated kinship. At times, what lies before our eyes is indeed a mirror of what dwells within us — the scattered notes, much like scattered thoughts; the half-finished letters like emotions not yet spoken.

Yet serenity is a strange and subtle thing. A person might sit before a sea of papers and still feel a calm as deep as the waters of the Golden Horn at dawn. For in such a case, the chaos is not confusion but companion — each paper a familiar voice, each ink blot a remembered hour, all of them arranged in a pattern only the keeper knows. This quiet comprehension can be as serene as the gentle order of a monk’s cell.

Tell me, my friend… how is it that a sound that once lulled a man to dreams can, years later, come to weigh on his chest like a sleepless stone?

You see, our experience of sound is not only about the ear — it is about the web of memories, emotions, and even the state of the body in that particular season of life. When we are younger, the mind can turn a dripping eave or the drum of rain on the tiles into a cradle-song, because our hearts are light and our inner rooms uncluttered. But as the years pass, that same rhythm can awaken what lies hidden — thoughts left unresolved, absences we still count, or simply a body that no longer finds rest as easily.

In the stillness of night, the senses sharpen. What once was a soft, distant murmur might now feel like an insistent tapping, pulling you away from the quiet you wish for within. The rain itself has not changed — but we have. Our past selves heard it through one window, our present selves through another.

There is also the truth that sounds carry the seasons of our own story. If a certain chapter of life was heavy and it rained much during those days, the ear may keep the association long after those clouds have gone. It’s a little like how an old song once danced to at a wedding can bring tears years later, if the people from that dance are gone.

Some elders say this is a mercy — the soul telling us gently to listen inward more than outward in certain hours. Others might say it is simply the passing of taste, like a favorite sherbet in youth that now feels too sweet on the tongue.

So perhaps, Mehmet Bey, the sound of the rain is still a lullaby… just being sung to a different man than the young fellow who once fell asleep to it.

Tell me, my friend, when did folks first start arranging those little word grids with the black and white squares… and was it always just for testing the mind, or was there another purpose in the beginning?

Ah, Mehmet Bey, those little black‑and‑white grids have a more recent history than one might expect. The invention of what we now call the modern crossword puzzle can be traced to December 21, 1913, in the Sunday edition of the New York World newspaper. A British-born journalist, Arthur Wynne, published what he called a 'Word-Cross' — a diamond-shaped arrangement of empty squares with clues, devised partly to entertain readers during the Christmas season.  

But here is the interesting nuance: at the beginning, it was seen less as a test of the mind in the competitive sense, and more as a form of light amusement — a cousin to the riddle, a gentle way to pass the time on a winter evening. In early decades, especially in America and Britain, it was linked to the leisurely rituals of tea-time or Sunday rest, rather like how our elders here would gather to exchange riddles, proverbs, and tongue‑twisters after the day’s work.  

By the 1920s and 1930s, publishers discovered that crosswords not only sold papers but also encouraged people to carry them about, marking them up over the day. Some even saw them as a mild social glue — commuters swapping clues, friends teasing each other over obscure answers. It was only in later decades, as the grids grew more intricate, that they began to attract a reputation as serious mental exercise, a test of vocabulary, lateral thinking, and quick wit.  

In that sense, their earliest spirit was closer to a parlor game than a battleground of intellect. If you imagine it — in a modest home by a coal stove, someone leaning over the paper and calling out, 'What is the eight-letter word for a sea bird?' — you can still feel the hum of simple, shared amusement rather than the strain of a solitary contest. So while today’s crosswords might sometimes feel like climbing a steep hill in the rain, their roots lie in something far lighter, almost like the folk riddles that carry the laughter of a whole room.
Tell me, my friend, is there a reason why some afternoons feel longer than others, even when the sun sinks at the same hour?

In the hours after midday, the human body often experiences a gentle drop in alertness — what scientists call the ‘post-prandial dip.’ It can be tied to our circadian rhythm: the internal clock that synchronizes with light, temperature, and our daily habits. For many, this is the time when eyelids grow heavy and the world feels slower. But when one passes through these hours without closing the eyes for a short rest, the mind may stretch the moment, making the shadows seem longer and the hours more lingering.

There is also the matter of how we occupy this time. If we are engaged in lively talk, busy hands, or a pleasant walk, the afternoon may still flow swiftly, like water over stones. But if we sit quietly, perhaps at the teahouse door watching the dust dance in the sunbeams, the moments can seem to lengthen, each second taking on the fullness of its own story. Memory affects it too — a mind recalling old springs and harvests often lingers over the present day, weighing it against the golden past, and in the process making it feel longer.

So, it is not always the sun that decides the length of an afternoon, but the tempo of your thoughts, the state of your body, and how you choose to cross those hours. Some afternoons are measured by the clock, others by the heart.
Tell me, my friend, why do some clouds seem to stay in one place while others hurry away?

Ah, Mehmet Bey, what you are noticing is the silent dance between earth and sky — and perhaps also a small illusion played on our eyes. When you stand still on the ground and lift your gaze up, some clouds truly are moving quickly, especially the lighter, lower ones, often the cumulus or stratus types that are carried by brisk winds nearer the surface. They can race along like anxious travelers late to catch a caravan.

But higher above, sometimes more than six or seven kilometers into the heavens, there are other kinds of clouds — cirrus, thin as fine muslin — drifting in far gentler currents, or in directions where the wind is slower, almost hesitant. They can seem to float in place simply because the wind around them is calm, or it moves in the same direction you are facing, keeping them framed against the same piece of distant sky.

There is also a kind of trick of perspective: when a cloud is very far away, over the mountains perhaps, its movement may be so small relative to your point of view that it looks frozen — like a white sail on the horizon that seems to hover. In truth, the whole sky is in motion, layer upon layer, with winds at different heights weaving unseen patterns. Meteorologists call this the *wind shear*, and it is why one layer of clouds might scurry past while another lounges like a guest unwilling to leave.

In our old village tales, the slow clouds were once said to be the 'thinking ones' — carrying long, heavy dreams of rain or snow, waiting for the right moment to share their burden with the earth. The quick ones were the 'messengers', darting ahead to herald a change in weather.

It is an old truth, Mehmet Bey, that the sky holds its own pace. Some days, the hurried clouds remind us of life’s fleeting moments; others, the still ones teach us the patience of watching. Even if you do not pause for them often, they pass overhead all the same, like quiet friends who need no words to keep you company.
